item.title: Are Wine Moms Rebelling or Surrendering?
item.description:
Parenting

Are Wine Moms Rebelling or Surrendering?

Drinking wine to stay afloat may be exactly what's pulling moms under.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Moms are working harder than ever to meet societal standards grounded in “intensive mothering ideology."
  • Wine mom culture offers burnt-out moms a community of escapism, which is not of help in the long term.
  • Moms devoting all resources to their kids feel drained and de-individualized, making survival the goal.
  • Moms and their allies can fight for change, eliminating the need to "escape" in the first place.

Contemporary mothers—myself not excluded—are exhausted by the constant, futile pursuit of society's unmeetable expectations.

"Wine mom" culture offers much-needed community to participants who—together, alone, and across social media landscapes—celebrate alcohol as a means of temporarily escaping their stress-ridden lives. It works, at least in the short term.

In the long term, though, when an effective coping mechanism makes an unbearable system bearable (and, let's be honest, kind of "fun"), why would anyone fight for change?

What Exactly Are (Wine) Moms Trying to Escape?

Source: Miller Inna / Shutterstock

Moms are expected to "do it all" without adequate support across institutional, policy, or community levels. Of course, the maternal mental health crisis is upon us. It is understandable why moms may take comfort in a glass of something cold, a community that "gets it," and a mass, destigmatized, rebranded-in-pink-glitter urge to disappear.

I wonder, though, what exactly are moms trying to disappear from? The whole mothering gig? One bad week? A burnt dinner?

When my partner and I decided to have children, I anticipated motherhood would have its challenges. What I did not anticipate was how thoroughly society's ideas around "good" mothering would infiltrate my values system. It happened ever so quietly, and with the stealth of a carbon monoxide leak: colorless, odorless, and extremely dangerous.

The belief system that has so insidiously woven its way into the fabric of our culture is "intensive mothering ideology," or IMI. I would argue that this credo, equal parts powerful and invisible, is the real villain of this story and the actual thing moms seek to escape—even if they have never heard of it.

IMI theorizes that a child's developmental outcome is entirely the product of maternal effort, devotion, vigilance, and self-sacrifice (Hays, 1996). It defines the "ideal" mother as one who devotes copious amounts of time, energy, and resources to her children; remains constantly available to them (physically and emotionally); and accepts primary responsibility for their overall development and well-being (Ennis, 2014).

IMI replaces moms' individual, holistic values with a blind devotion to the "more is more" mentality, one that is notably and negatively impacting the mental health of mothers and the children they are raising.

A (Very) Brief History of Intensive Mothering

Source: Everett Collection / Shutterstock

The standards of "good" mothering that have fed into IMI have been passed down from generation to generation since the 17th century (Hays, 1996).

This belief system's grip tightened in the mid-20th century when Bowlby's attachment research rose to prominence and being a "good" mother became synonymous with an intensive, "child-centered" approach to parenting (Bretherton, 1992).

Winnicott's (1960) "good-enough mother" theory had the potential to change the conversation, as it offered a more sustainable vision of mothering that acknowledged the individual wants and needs of mothers, and posited that children benefit from age-appropriate exposure to frustration.

Unfortunately, Winnicott's work never achieved the same cultural traction as Bowlby's. Many believe that because Bowlby's work subscribed to a gendered narrative that benefited the patriarchy, and because men occupied (and still occupy) positions of power, the widespread expectations of mothers were (and are) bound to favor theories that do not threaten the gender status quo.

IMI remains the dominant discourse around "good" mothering, urging moms to fight an unwinnable battle for perfection at the cost of their entire selves.

General Critiques of Wine Mom Culture

Most criticisms of wine mom culture are related to the health risks of alcohol use—for example, the danger of "wine is a form of 'earned' self-care" messaging for mothers predisposed to addiction, or the recklessness of normalizing alcohol as a stress management tool without addressing potential negative consequences (Davey, 2023).

These concerns certainly hold statistical water, yet that is not to say all moms must stop drinking wine.

In the science of addiction, the difference between someone who uses substances and someone who abuses substances comes down to the function of the use. For wine moms, alcohol is problematic because it functions as an avoidance mechanism, thereby posing significant mental health threats.

With an understanding of the World Health Organization's stance that there is no such thing as safe alcohol consumption, moms may choose to engage in moderate, minimally problematic drinking by remaining mindful of associated risks and asking themselves—often—whether alcohol is being relied on to tolerate something that would otherwise be intolerable.

A gift from a well-meaning friend when I had my third kid.
Source: Ali KL

The Sober Mom's Qualms

Sober mom communities have been paying close attention to wine mom culture, and they have some concerns.

One feature they take issue with is how wine mom communities are built. Sober moms point out that connection organized around a shared coping mechanism is, by design, surface-level. It bonds women over exhaustion, performative social media posts, and escapism rather than values, vision, or a genuine shared desire for something better.

Research on recovery from alcoholism suggests that the shift from alcohol-centered connection to clear-headed, reciprocally respectful relationships is not just personally meaningful; it is transformative (Pettersen et al., 2023). For moms, that could mean feeling their feelings, not numbing them, and engaging in dialogue around what they are experiencing and what structural changes may be worth fighting for.

Sober moms also offer critiques from a feminist perspective. For example, they report that sobriety opens their eyes not just to the limits of wine mom culture, but to the broader systems of coercion and subjugation that have kept women, and mothers specifically, in subordinate roles (Davey, 2023).

In this vein, they criticize the language and imagery associated with wine moms for being hyperfeminine to the extent that it can be perceived as child-like. They suggest this infantilizes moms and minimizes their very real struggles. They also believe this branding choice was intentional as a way to foster "safe," socially acceptable acts of defiance while removing any indication of threat to the patriarchy.

Source: Reetha Ferguson / Pexels

The Buzz of a New Discourse

What might it look like to bring moms together around something other than shared depletion and a "well-deserved" pour?

It might start with naming IMI and recognizing that it does not apply equally to all mothers. Researchers note that intensive mothering discourse consistently fails to reflect the realities of mothers who are not white, middle-class, and resource-equipped: mothers of color, low-income mothers, working mothers, and LGBTQ+ mothers whose distinct experiences are largely absent from IMI's innately hetero-gendered framework (Newman & Nelson, 2021). A new discourse must cover more diverse ground than the one it replaces.

It might represent aspects of "extensive mothering," a framework described by Karen Christopher in which mothers are encouraged to nurture all aspects of their whole identities, so long as their children's needs are being met. Notably, many mothers who privately aligned with extensive mothering said they would not endorse it publicly for fear of being labeled a "bad mom" (Christopher, 2012). The silence keeping that fear in place is exactly what a new discourse would dismantle.

It might involve new mom communities that more closely mirror the deeper, healthier ones sober moms are already building.

It might not involve the decision to numb our collective emotions, thereby disabling our deep, desperate need for increased support.

It might mirror the countries that have made systemic changes to support mothers, including paid parental leave, subsidized childcare, flexible work structures, and genuine community-building infrastructure. Moms in these countries are not facing the same mental health crises we see in the U.S., and the difference is not the quality of the mothers; it is the quality of the system they are mothering in.

Source: Jihan Nafiaa Zahri / Shutterstock

Now What?

Surviving the toxic version of motherhood society has imposed on us by accepting it as inevitable cannot, and will not, be enough.

This is not a call for mothers to stop drinking wine. It is an invitation to get curious about when and why we are reaching for it, and to think carefully about participating in a cultural trend that, however comforting in the short term, maintains a broken system.

We do not need more "Mama Needs Her Special Juice!" T-shirts. We need the promise of real, long-term relief, the kind that comes from a shift in how we talk about "good" mothering, from long-overdue institutional support, and from permission to nurture the parts of our identities that exist outside of "mom."

We deserve to mother within a structure that makes coping unnecessary.

item.title: AI and the Two Forms of Authorship
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Two Forms of Authorship

Personal Perspective: AI Is separating two things we never had to tell apart.

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Writing used to mean the thinker and the writer were the same person.
  • AI can now write fluent sentences with no lived experience.
  • The question isn't who gets credit, but if we can tell if there's a mind behind it.
Source: Image by Valerio Errani from Pixabay.

The author.

Looking back, that word carried a single and powerful claim. The author was the one who had the thought and wrote it down. It was the same person and the act without a gap between them. This is what gave writing its authority. It wasn't just the elegance of the sentence, but the assumption that a mind stood behind it. Importantly, being a writer was inexorably connected to being a thinker.

AI may be the first technology with the power to separate the two.

Start with what we can see. Linguistic authorship is the words themselves. It's the structure and phrasing that carries an idea off from one mind to another. You can point to a well-crafted sentence and admire it for only its construction. And for a long time, that visibility was enough, because the words were the only evidence we had of the human mind that produced them.

Good sentences implied good thinking. We had no reason to doubt this inference.

Source: ChatGPT modified by NostaLab.

Cognitive authorship is different, and much harder to see. It's the judgment that decided which idea mattered combined with the reasoning that shaped it. None of this appears on the page. We trusted that it had happened, because the words in front of us seemed to require, if not demand, it.

Today, an LLM can produce linguistic authorship that is both competent and elegant. But I'll argue that there's no cognitive authorship behind it at all. Yes, there's a statistical power that shapes the sentences and mimics thought. But there's no resistance or personal cost—just output. And yet the sentence seems like someone agonized over every word. This is the part that we, you and I, need to think about.

Textual fluency stopped being evidence of anything.

I say this as someone who uses these LLMs daily. I bring formed and half-baked ideas to a model and ask it to test them in iterative dialogue. That's not nothing, but I don't think it's quite writing either, at least not in the traditional sense where the sentence and the thought arrived together. I notice the difference. I'm not always sure the reader really can.

Maybe that's the real question the diagram is forcing us to confront. It's not who gets credit for the words on the page, but whether we can still tell when a mind was actually behind it. In the past, we didn't have to ask. But today, we may not get to avoid it much longer.

item.title: America on a GLP-1: A Field Guide to 2030
item.description:
Health

America on a GLP-1: A Field Guide to 2030

GLP-1s now change individual minds. What happens when they change 40 million?

Posted July 30, 2026

Key points
  • Like smartphones and internet use, GLP-1 medicines are rapidly being adopted in the U.S.
  • As usage increases, GLP-1 driven changes will scale from the individual to the broader society.
  • GLP-1 medicines will impact society from young to old, across physical, mental, social, and cultural areas.

Rosa stood at the jeweler's counter and held out her hand for the second time in three years.

"Same ring?" the jeweler asked, though he already knew the answer. He'd resized it for her once before, 18 months into her GLP-1 journey, when it had started slipping past her knuckle at the grocery store. Now it was loose again. "Business has never been better," he said, almost apologetically, sliding it onto the sizing mandrel. He didn't have to explain what he meant. Half his appointments these days were some version of this.

Rosa didn't think much of it at the time. But it was also a sign that something was happening. Something much larger than her own hand.

Source: Thomas Rutledge/PowerPoint

The Coming GLP-1 Tsunami

In 2024, about 3 percent of U.S. adults were taking a GLP-1 medication for weight loss. Two years later, that number soared to 11 percent, with 15 percent (almost 1 in 6 people) reporting having used one at some point. Some projections put usage at 13 percent to 21 percent of U.S. adults within the next several years—somewhere between 30 and 50 million people. Whatever the exact figure turns out to be, the direction is not in question.1

GLP-1 medicines affect more than waistlines. For many, their psychosocial effects are equally profound: food noise, mental health, relationships, the very sense of who someone is becoming. But as these individual transformations scale into the collective population, it's worth asking: If a single brain can be changed this much, what happens when tens of millions of brains change in the same direction?

Consider this question the way you might think of a piece written in 1995 called "America on the Internet." Nobody in 1995 correctly predicted everything. Nobody guessed Amazon, or Zoom, or a smartphone in every pocket. Some of what follows will look obvious in hindsight. Some of it will look a little ridiculous. That's the nature of reading the tea leaves this early. We're writing it anyway, because the fun is in the forecasting, not in getting every detail right.

Ozempic Shopping

On her way home, Rosa stopped at the store she's shopped at for 20 years. It didn't look like it used to. The produce section had expanded, the dairy case had grown, and an entire new refrigerated wall was devoted to preportioned lean proteins that hadn't existed the last time she'd really paid attention. The center aisles—the ones previously filled with chips and cookies and soda — had visibly shrunk. Her own cart, she realized, looked nothing like the one she used to push. Neither did anyone else's.

article continues after advertisement

This is the least surprising part of the 2030 forecast: Fast-food chains quietly rolling out smaller, protein-packed menu options (call it the "Ozempic Burger" effect). Apparel racks shifting toward smaller sizes while resale shops boom with the larger clothes people are shedding. Airlines saving millions on fuel as average passenger weight drops. None of this requires a crystal ball. It's already underway.2

Ozempic-Era Status Symbols

Here's where the future gets murkier. For most of the last century, a thinner body functioned as a status symbol for self-discipline, higher income, and healthy values. By 2030, GLP-1 medicines will have made that signal available by prescription. But when a scarce status symbol becomes common, the human desire for status isn't erased. It evolves.

Expect factors such as muscle tone, physical strength, and fitness to fill this status symbol void. Not just "thin," but a body that projects weight lifting, vigorous training, and disciplined nutrition. Strong and fit will become the new thin, the new status symbol for people who can afford the trainer, the time, and the food on top of the medicine. Don't be surprised if a countertrend emerges too, prizing bodies that look unaltered and "natural" as their own kind of rare, expensive signal (like billionaires wearing T-shirts and casual sweaters do today). Status always finds a way to reveal itself.

Ozempic Dating

Significant weight loss doesn't just change how people see themselves; it changes how they date. Expect the emergence of social media platforms and meetup communities built specifically around shared GLP-1 experience, something like a "NewYou" or a "SizeMatters" app, where the appeal isn't just meeting someone, but meeting someone who understands exactly this kind of life journey. Expect social disclosure norms to evolve as well. "Are you on a GLP-1?" may become as normal a first date question as anything about kids, jobs, or politics.

Ozempic Retirement

The 65+ generation is the group currently most disabled by obesity and weight-related health conditions. Empowered by GLP-1 medicines in 2030, however, retiring people will enjoy greater physical capacity—for travel, for hiking, for standing in a garden for four hours without their knees complaining—at precisely the life stage when they finally have the leisure hours to spend.3

article continues after advertisement

Call it "Ozempic retirement": newfound physical freedom arriving with no job obligation to oppose it. The open question is whether communities, travel companies, and senior living operators build collaboratively for this, or whether it happens the way most big social shifts happen—individually, industry by industry, years behind the people actually living the change.

Ozempic Healthcare

Even universal GLP-1 access will not ensure equal health outcomes. As in the present, in 2030, people will experience different levels of healthcare quality. At one end: GLP-1 script-only care, a prescription and a checkup, nothing more. At the other: the GLP-1 boutique—full-stack care bundling a physician, wearable tech, a psychologist, a personal trainer, and a dietitian into one coordinated program. The medicine may be the same. The results won't be. The currently unequal American healthcare model will remain just that, only in novel forms.4

The Ozempic Generation

Two threads collide here. Both are already happening. GLP-1 medicines are restoring ovulation in women who weren't ovulating regularly, producing a documented rise in unplanned pregnancies already nicknamed "Ozempic babies."5 At the other end of childhood, semaglutide and liraglutide are FDA-approved for adolescents 12 and older; adolescent use has climbed roughly sixfold in five years, and fewer than 1 percent of eligible teens are now using one. The latter means this potentially seismic shift for American youth has just barely started.6

Call the cohort now growing up alongside this medicine the "Ozempic generation": kids whose relationship with hunger, bodies, and food may look profoundly different from their parents', raised by parents and schools that are mostly improvising as they go. Expect pediatricians, school nurses, and parenting podcasts to spend the next decade catching up.

article continues after advertisement

Ozempic Holidays: When Food Isn't the Centerpiece

These changes will show up in the minor corners of daily life as well as the major. Rosa's ring is one example of the former—jewelers specialized in ring resizing invisibly becoming a growth industry to serve millions of new customers. And her Sunday social plans now involve a hike and picnic with a friend instead of a sit-down restaurant meal.

Expect major holidays to feel the shift too. Picture a Charlie Brown Christmas for the GLP-1 era: not just a small and simple tree, but now an equally modest and less processed meal alongside it. Dinner table rituals shift toward spending less time on second helpings and more on conversation, with a Thanksgiving less centered on cooking, eating, and cleaning up, and more centered on connecting and creating memories.

Ozempic Living

GLP-1 medicine use started with physical health: obesity, diabetes, and other metabolic diseases. But as these medicines mature, expect the emphasis to shift steadily from weight loss toward something broader: wellness, longevity, healthspan, and quality of life, especially for middle-aged and older adults. GLP-1 journeys now focused on generic medical goals will evolve increasingly toward personalized goals.

Rosa drove home with her ring fitting properly again, thinking about the road trip she had planned this weekend with a friend. Neither felt like a headline. For her, both had quietly become routine.
